description: We’re Orbit Ember Labs, a team interested in web development and machine learning. We’re building FlameBrief, a tool that helps users compare NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments and explore the original reports. We’re looking for teammates who can help with data analysis, UI design, or presenting the project.
summary: FlameBrief helps researchers and students explore how fire behaves in spacecraft. Built for the Flame in Freefall challenge, it brings NASA combustion reports into a searchable experiment library, a measurement desk, five interactive simulation stations, and a research chat with citations. Users can compare how airflow affects flame spread, examine smoke detection studies, and replay the visible extinction of fuel droplets. Every reported measurement can be traced to a NASA source. By showing where experimental evidence ends and model assumptions begin, FlameBrief helps users identify what still needs to be tested before applying ISS findings to future missions.
details:
FlameBrief connects NASA combustion measurements to questions about spacecraft fire prevention, detection, and suppression. The experiment library ranks 17 records by topic and mission environment. The research archive contains 1,094 searchable passages from 15 documents. Users can compare test conditions, download CSV files, and follow citations to the original reports.

The laboratory has five stations covering flame spread, cabin gases, droplet extinction, smoke transport, and cabin atmosphere. The first three use selected BASS-II, Saffire VI, and FLEX measurements. The smoke transport and cabin atmosphere stations use simplified models. For example, the FLEX station interpolates between reported droplet diameters and ends at visible flame extinction. The lunar smoke detection example points users to SAME, SAME-R, and ASE while identifying where lunar test data is still needed.

The public research chat retrieves NASA sources and returns cited findings and exact measurements. FlameBrief was built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Node.js and is hosted on Vercel. The intended impact is to make NASA combustion evidence easier to find, compare, and use when planning further experiments.
